description: The canonical byte encoding of a command's signed content. Unlike every other file here, these cases pin an ENCODING rather than a DECISION: two implementations can agree that a signature is invalid while disagreeing about what bytes a valid one covers, and that disagreement is invisible until a phone and a desktop are paired.
encoding: Each of the four fields is emitted in the fixed order sender, command, createdAtMillis, nonce. Each is prefixed by its byte length as a 4-byte big-endian unsigned integer, followed by that many bytes: UTF-8 for the three strings, ASCII decimal digits for createdAtMillis. Length prefixes rather than a delimiter, because a delimiter is forgeable — see the boundary-ambiguity pair below.

cases.description: An ordinary command. The baseline every other case varies from.

A sender identifier containing multi-byte UTF-8. The length prefix counts BYTES, not characters or code points — an implementation prefixing the character count produces a different encoding here while agreeing on every ASCII case.

A nonce containing the pipe and colon a naive encoder would have joined fields with. Under a delimiter encoding this value would split one field into several; under length prefixing it is ordinary data with no special meaning.

First half of the pair that proves the encoding is unambiguous. Sender 'ab' with nonce 'c'. Its encoding MUST differ from boundary-ambiguity-sender-a-nonce-bc — if the two match, the encoding is forgeable and an attacker can move bytes across a field boundary while keeping a valid signature.
Second half of the pair. Sender 'a' with nonce 'bc' — the same concatenated characters as the case above, divided differently. Distinct field values MUST produce distinct bytes.

The Unix epoch itself, encoded as the single digit 0 rather than as a fixed-width or padded number. Pins that the instant is rendered as decimal millis with no padding, so an implementation zero-filling to a fixed width fails here.
